metadata.title: Formalization of de Rham cohomologies of a smooth manifold

nodes.statement: A \emph{continuous alternating map} from \(E^{I}\) to \(F\), where \(E\) and \(F\) are topological vector spaces over a nontrivially normed field \(\mathbb k\) and \(I\) is an index type (usually, \texttt{Fin n} for some \(n\)), is a map \(f\colon E^{I} \to F\) such that \begin{itemize} \item \(f(x_{1}, \dots, x_{n - 1})\) is linear in each variable \(x_{i}\); \item \(f\) is a continuous map. \end{itemize}
nodes.label: def:cont-alt-map

nodes.statement: If \(E\) is a seminormed space over \(\mathbb k\) and \(F\) is a (semi)normed space over \(\mathbb k\), then \(k\)-alternating maps from \(E\) to \(F\) form a (semi)normed space over \(\mathbb k\). The addition and scalar multiplication are pointwise, and the norm is given by \begin{equation} \|f\| = \operatorname{Inf} \left\{C \mid C \ge 0 \wedge \forall m, \|f(m)\| \le C\prod_{i=0}^{k-1}\|m_{i}\|\right\}. \end{equation}
nodes.label: thm:normed-grp

nodes.statement: The statement immediately follows from a similar statement about continuous multilinear maps.

If \(g\colon F \to G\) is a continuous linear map between topological vector spaces over \(\mathbb k\) and \(f\colon E^{I} \to F\) is a continuous alternating map, then \(g \circ f\colon E^{I}\to G\) is a continuous alternating map.
nodes.label: thm:clm-comp

nodes.statement: This fact immediately follows from the definitions.

If \(g\colon F^{I} \to G\) is a continuous alternating map and \(f\colon E \to F\) is a continuous linear map then \(f^{*}g \colon E^{I} \to G\) given by \(f^{*}g(\dots, x_{j}, \dots) = g (\dots, f(x_{j}), \dots)\) is a continuous alternating map.
nodes.label: thm:comp-clm

nodes.statement: If \(g\colon F^{I} \to G\) is a continuous alternating map with nonempty \(I\) (e.g., \(g\colon F^{k}\to G\) and \(k > 0\)), then \(0^{*}g = 0\), where \(0\colon E \to F\) is the zero map.
nodes.label: lem:comp-clm-zero

nodes.statement: If \(I\) is an empty type (e.g., \(\mathrm{Fin} 0\)), then the map sending the unique element of \(E^{I}\) to a constant \(c\) is a continuous alternating map. Moreover, this construction provides a continuous linear equivalence \(mk_0\) between \(F\) and continuous alternating maps \(E^{I} \to G\).
nodes.label: def:cont-alt-map-zero

nodes.statement: If \(I\) has a unique element \(i\) (e.g., \(I = \mathrm{Fin} 1\) and \(i = 0\)), then continuous alternating maps from \(E^{I}\) to \(F\) are just continuous linear maps from \(E\) to \(F\). The equivalence is given by \(mk_1\).
nodes.label: def:cont-alt-map-one

nodes.statement: If the domain \(E\) is a finite dimensional topological vector space with Hausdorff topology, then any multilinear map from \(E\) is continuous.
nodes.label: thm:cont-mult-map-findim

nodes.statement: If the domain \(E\) is a finite dimensional topological vector space with Hausdorff topology, then any alternating map from \(E\) is continuous.
nodes.label: thm:cont-alt-map-findim

nodes.statement: The proof immediately follows from \autoref{thm:cont-mult-map-findim} and the fact that an alternating map is a multilinear map.

If \(f\colon E^{k + 1} \to F\) is a continuous alternating map and \(v\) is a vector, then \(f_{v}\colon E^{k} \to F\) given by \[ f_{v}(x_{0}, \dots, x_{k - 1})=f(v, x_{0}, \dots, x_{k - 1}) \] is a \(k\)-alternating map. Moreover, this map is linear in \(f\) and \(v\). We will use notation \(curry_1 f\) for the map sending \(v\) to \(f_{v}\).
nodes.label: def:cont-alt-curry-fin

nodes.statement: Let \(f\colon E^{k + l} \to F\) be a continuous alternating map. For each vector \(x \in E^{k}\), the formula \[ \left(\mathrm{curry}_{k,l} f(x)\right)(y) = f(x, y) \] defines a continuous alternating map \(E^{l}\to F\). Moreover, this function is linear in \(f\) and is multilinear in \(x\).
nodes.label: def:cont-alt-curry-fin-add

nodes.statement: Let \(f\colon E^{k + 1}\to F\) be a continuous multilinear map which is alternating in all but the first variable. Formally, we represent this as \(f\) being a continuous linear map on \(E\) taking values in the space of continuous alternating maps \(E^{k}\to F\). Define the \emph{uncurrying} or \emph{\(1\)-alternatization} of \(f\) to be the continuous alternating map given by \[ alt_1(f)(x_{0}, \dots, x_{k}) = \sum_{j=0}^{k}{(-1)}^{j}f(x_{j}, x_{0}, \dots, \widehat{x_{j}}, \dots, x_{k}), \] where \(\widehat{x_{j}}\) means that \(x_{j}\) is removed from the sequence. Here \({(-1)}^{j}\) is the sign of the cyclic permutation \((0, \dots, j)\).
nodes.label: def:alt-one

nodes.statement: If \(f\) is a continuous \(k\)-alternating map, then \(alt_1(curry_1 f) = (k + 1)f\).
nodes.label: thm:uncurry-curry-one

nodes.statement: The map \(alt_1(f)\) defined above is continuous and linear in \(f\).
nodes.label: lem:alt-one-linear

nodes.statement: Linearity follows from the definition. Continuity follows from the inequality \(\|alt_1(f)(x)\|\le (k + 1)\|f\|\prod_{j}\|x_{j}\|\).
We do not divide the result of \autoref{def:alt-one} by \(k + 1\) to ensure that it works if \(\mathbb k\) has a positive characteristic.
Let \(f\colon E^{k + 2}\to F\) be a continuous multilinear map which is alternating in all but the first two variables. If \(f\) is symmetric in the first two variables, then \(alt_1(alt_1(f)) = 0\).
nodes.label: thm:uncurry2-eq-zero

nodes.statement: Let \(f\colon E^{k + l}\to F\) be a continuous multilinear map which is alternating in the first \(k\) argument and in the other \(l\) arguments. Then \(\mathrm{altAdd}_{k,l}(f)\) is the continuous alternating map given by \[ \mathrm{altAdd}_{k,l}(f)(x_{0}, \dots, x_{k + l - 1})=\sum_{\substack{s\subseteq [0, k + l)\\|s|=k}}{(-1)}^{\mathrm{sign} \sigma_{s}}f(\sigma_{s}(0), \dots, \sigma_{s}(k + l - 1)), \] where for each \(k\)-element set \(s\), \(\sigma_{s}\) is a permutation of \(\mathrm{Fin} (k + l)\) that sends \(s\) to \([0, k)\) and its complement to \([k, k + l)\). The exact choice of \(\sigma_{s}\) is not important, but we choose the permutation that is monotone both on \(s\) and on its complement.
nodes.label: def:uncurry-fin-add

nodes.statement: If \(k = 1\), then \(\mathrm{altAdd}_{1, l}(mk_1(f)) = \mathrm{altAdd}_{1}(f)\).
nodes.label: thm:uncurry-fin-add-one

nodes.statement: If \(f\) is a continuous alternating map, then \(\mathrm{curry}_{k, l}(\mathrm{altAdd}_{k, l}(f)) = \binom{k + l}{k}f\).
nodes.label: thm:curry-uncurry-fin-add

nodes.statement: Consider a continuous bilinear map \(f \colon E' \times F' \to G\) and continuous alternating maps \(g\colon E^{I}\to E'\) and \(h\colon F^{J}\to F'\). Then the formula \[ f \circ_{2} (g, h)(v, w) = f(g(v), h(w)) \] defines a continuous multilinear map \(E^{I}\times F^{J}\to G\) which is alternating both in the first \(I\) variables and in the other \(J\) variables.
nodes.label: def:clm-comp2-cam

nodes.statement: Let \(f \colon F \times G \to H\) be a continuous bilinear map. Let \(\omega \colon E^{k} \to F\) and \(\eta\colon E^{l}\to G\) be continuous alternating maps. Then the \emph{wedge product} of \(\omega\) and \(\eta\) with respect to \(f\) is given by \[ \omega \wedge_{f} \eta = \mathrm{altAdd}_{k, l}(f \circ_{2}(g, h)). \]
nodes.label: def:cam-wedge

nodes.statement: Wedge product \(\omega \wedge_{f} \eta\) is linear in \(f\), \(\omega\), and \(\eta\).
nodes.label: thm:wedge-clm3

nodes.statement: The wedge product is associative\todo{Add a version for \(\omega \wedge_{f}\eta\); we'll need several spaces and continuous bilinear maps here}, \((\omega_{1}\wedge \omega_{2})\wedge \omega_{3} = \omega_{1}\wedge (\omega_{2}\wedge \omega_{3})\). Note that in Lean the sides have different types as \((k + l) + m = k + (l + m)\) is not a definitional equality, so the formalized statement involves a natural isomorphism.
nodes.label: thm:wedge-assoc

nodes.statement: If \(a\) is a vector and \(\omega\) is a continuous alternating map, then \(mk_0 a \wedge_{f} \omega = f(a) \circ \omega\).
nodes.label: thm:mk0-wedge-bilin

nodes.statement: If \(a\) is a number and \(\omega\) is a continuous alternating map, then \(mk_0 a \wedge \omega = a\omega\).
nodes.label: thm:mk0-wedge

nodes.statement: This theorem immediately follows from \autoref{thm:mk0-wedge-bilin}.

If \(\omega\colon E^{k}\to F\) and \(\eta\colon E^{l}\to G\) are continuous alternating maps and \(f \colon F \times G \to H\) is a continuous bilinear map, then \(\omega \wedge_{f} \eta = {(-1)}^{kl}\eta \wedge_{f'} \omega\), where \(f'(y, x) = f(x, y)\). Note that the LHS and the RHS have different types in Lean, so the actual statement involves a natural isomorphism.
nodes.label: thm:wedge-comm

nodes.statement: Let \(\omega\colon E^{2}\to \mathbb R\) be a skew-symmetric bilinear map on a vector space of dimension \(2k\). Then \(\omega\wedge\dots\wedge\omega = 0\) iff the corresponding matrix has determinant zero. \todo{We may need \(n\)-ary version of the wedge product to define this. Or should we just define the power by induction?}
nodes.label: thm:wedge-pow-zero-iff-det

nodes.statement: The \emph{pullback} of \(\omega\in \Omega^{k}(F, G)\) along a map \(f\colon E\to F\) within a set \(s\) is the \(k\)-form \(f_{s}^{*}\omega\) given by \(f_{s}^{*}\omega(x) = {(d_{s}f(x))}^{*}\omega(f(x))\), where \(d_{s}f(x)\) is the Fréchet derivative of \(f\) within \(s\) at \(x\), and the right-hand side is defined in~\autoref{thm:comp-clm}.
nodes.label: def:pullback-within

nodes.statement: If \(f\colon E\to F\) is not differentiable within \(s\) at \(x\) and \(k > 0\), then \(f_{s}^{*}\omega(x)=0\) for any \(k\)-form \(\omega\).
nodes.label: lem:pullback-within-of-non-diff

nodes.statement: This fact immediately follows from \autoref{lem:comp-clm-zero} and the fact that \(d_{s}f(x)=0\). The latter is true because of the junk values Mathlib uses for derivatives.
The \emph{pullback} of \(\omega\in \Omega^{k}(F, G)\) along a map \(f\colon E\to F\) is the pullback of \(\omega\) along \(f\) within the universal set in the domain.
nodes.label: def:pullback-space

nodes.statement: The pullback \(f_{s}^{*}\omega\) within a set is a continuous linear map in \(\omega\).
nodes.label: thm:pullback-within-as-clm

nodes.statement: The pullback \(f^{*}\omega\) is a continuous linear map in \(\omega\).
nodes.label: thm:pullback-as-clm

nodes.statement: This fact immediately follows from \autoref{thm:pullback-within-as-clm}.

The pullback (within a set) of the \(0\)-form given by a function \(f\colon F\to G\) along a map \(g\colon E\to F\) is the \(0\)-form given by the function \(f\circ g\). Note that this statement is true even if \(g\) is not differentiable.
nodes.label: lem:pullback-within-mk0

nodes.statement: Given a map \(f\colon E\to F\), a set \(s \subset E\), a continuous alternating maps \(\omega\colon F^{k}\to G\), \(\eta\colon F^{l}\to G'\), and a continuous bilinear map \(g\colon G\times G' \to H\), we have \(f_{s}^{*}(\omega \wedge_{g}\eta) = f_{s}^{*}\omega\wedge_{g}f_{s}^{*}\eta\).
nodes.label: lem:pullback-within-wedge

nodes.statement: Consider a differential \(k\)-form \(\omega \in \Omega^{k}(E, F)\). By definition, its Fréchet derivative within a set \(s\) at a point \(x\) is a continuous linear map taking values in the space of continuous alternating maps from \(E^{k}\) to \(F\). The \emph{exterior derivative} of \(\omega\) \emph{within} \(s\) is the \((k + 1)\)-form \(d_{s}\omega\in\Omega^{k + 1}(E, F)\) that sends each \(x\) to the uncurrying of this Fréchet derivative.
nodes.label: def:ederivWithin

nodes.statement: The \emph{exterior derivative} of a differential \(k\)-form \(\omega\) is its exterior derivative within the universal set in the domain.
nodes.label: def:ederiv

nodes.statement: Assume that \(\omega\) is twice differentiable within \(s\) at \(x\) and the second derivatives commute. Then \(d_{s}(d_{s}\omega) = 0\). The latter condition automatically holds, if the base field is \(\mathbb R\) or \(\mathbb C\) and \(s\) is a convex set with nonempty interior.
nodes.label: def:ederivWithin-sq

nodes.statement: The pullback commutes with the exterior derivative. \todo[inline]{What are the exact assumptions?}
nodes.label: thm:pullback-ederiv-within

nodes.statement: For simplicity, we only prove this theorem for the non-restricted exterior derivative and pullback. Consider a differentiable function \(f\colon E \to F\) and a differentiable \(k\)-form \(\omega\in \Omega^{k}(F, G)\). Take \(k+1\) vectors \(X_{0}, \dots, X_{k}\in E\). Simplify both sides. \begin{align*} (f^{*}d\omega(a))(X_{0}, \dots, X_{k}) &=(d\omega)(f(a))(f_{*}(a)X_{0}, \dots, f_{*}(a)X_{k})\\ &=\sum_{j=0}^{k}{(-1)}^{j}\partial_{f_{*}(a)X_{j}}\omega(y)(\dots, \widehat{f_{*}(a)X_{j}}, \dots) \end{align*} OTOH, \begin{align*} d(f^{*}\omega)(a)(X_{0}, \dots, X_{k}) &=\sum_{j=0}^{k}{(-1)}^{j}\partial_{X_{j}}(f^{*}\omega)(\dots, \widehat{X_{j}}, \dots)\\ &=\sum_{j=0}^{k}{(-1)}^{j}\partial_{X_{j}}\left[\omega(f(x))(\dots, \widehat{f_{*}(x)X_{j}}, \dots)\right]\\ &=(f^{*}d\omega(a))(X_{0}, \dots, X_{k}) + \sum_{j=0}^{k}{(-1)}^{j}\partial_{X_{j}}\left[\omega(f(a))(\dots, \widehat{f_{*}(x)X_{j}}, \dots)\right]\\ \end{align*} \todo[inline]{It looks like we can prove a formula that implies both this and the formula for \(d\omega(X_{0}, \dots, X_{k})\), where \(X_{j}\) are vector fields.}
